title: China's CCTV affiliate attacks Anthropic's privacy policy over US intelligence sharing
subtitle: A social account tied to China Central Television called out Anthropic's latest privacy revision for allowing user data to reach US intelligence agencies without legal process, and flagged the language on the company's threat-intelligence job listings.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: A social media account affiliated with China Central Television — the country's main state broadcaster — published a critique on Friday, September 19, of Anthropic's most recent privacy-policy revision. The account said the new language allows Anthropic to share user data with US intelligence agencies 'when it deems necessary,' without the legal process usually required for such disclosures. It counted 13 revisions to Anthropic's privacy policy since 2023 and expansions in data sources from three categories to six between June 2024 and September 2025, and noted provisions that move data from users in Canada, Brazil, South Korea, and the European Union into the United States.

The post's most concrete point was about hiring. Two of the three threat-intelligence roles Anthropic is currently advertising give hiring preference to candidates with Mandarin or Russian language skills, government or military intelligence-analysis backgrounds, and active top-secret US security clearances. The CCTV account read that as evidence that Anthropic is now functioning, in part, as an extension of the US national-security apparatus — and pointed to the September 11 Anthropic threat-intelligence report, which named China and Iran among countries that had used Claude to support influence operations and spying, as the moment the mask came off.

The framing is state-media rhetoric, but the underlying facts check out and are non-trivial. Anthropic did publish that threat-intelligence report on September 11. It has expanded its threat-intelligence team and its US-government relationships throughout 2026 — recall the July Pentagon lift, the August Palantir integration, and the September Novo Nordisk deal. And its privacy policy does contain broad exceptions for national-security disclosures. For enterprise customers outside the United States, particularly in the EU and South Korea where cross-border transfer law is now actively enforced, this is a live procurement question, not a talking point.

Takeaway for learners — if you or your organization use a frontier AI vendor for anything sensitive, read the actual privacy policy, not the marketing page, and read it with the version-history diff turned on. Every major lab has quietly widened its 'we may share with law enforcement or intelligence agencies' clauses in the last twelve months. That doesn't make any single vendor uniquely bad, and it doesn't validate a state-media hit piece, but it does mean the assumptions you might have brought from 2024 — that a lab is a neutral technology provider — no longer hold. The vendors are actors in a national-security landscape now, and they have been for some time.
